f-date.claim: The battle of Salamis was fought in 480 BC, traditionally dated to late September.
cites: Barry Strauss, The Battle of Salamis (2004)

f-susa.claim: Xerxes sent a horseman to Susa to announce his success.

f-aeschylus-message.claim: Aeschylus, eight years later, also tells of a Greek who came to Xerxes saying the Greeks would slip away under cover of night.

f-throne-aigaleos.claim: Xerxes watched the battle seated at the foot of Mount Aigaleos, on the mainland opposite Salamis.

f-throne-scribes.claim: Whenever he saw one of his captains do something notable, he asked who it was, and his scribes wrote down the captain's name, his father and his city.

f-throne-golden.claim: Plutarch says Xerxes sat on a golden throne, with many secretaries beside him to record the battle.

f-artemisia.claim: Artemisia, queen of Halicarnassus, chased by an Athenian ship, rammed and sank a ship from her own side.

f-men-women.claim: Xerxes thought she had sunk a Greek ship and said: my men have become women, and my women men.

f-phoenicians.claim: When Phoenician captains blamed the Ionians for the defeat, Xerxes had them beheaded.

f-robes.claim: Aeschylus says that when Xerxes saw the depth of the disaster he tore his robes and cried out, for he had a seat in full view of the whole army, on a high hill near the sea.

f-narrows.claim: In the narrow strait the crowded Persian ships could not use their numbers; they struck each other with their bronze rams and broke their oars.

f-fleet-size.claim: Aeschylus puts the Greek fleet at about 310 ships and Xerxes' fleet at 1,207.
cites: Barry Strauss, The Battle of Salamis (2004)
